research_text:
## API and meaning of the finding

`javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec` represents a raw secret key, supplied as bytes and associated with an algorithm name, independently of a provider. The two constructors accept either the whole byte array or a specified slice. The reported value `DESede` therefore concerns the constructor’s **algorithm-name argument**, not the key bytes themselves. The diagnostic alone does not identify which constructor was observed or establish runtime behavior. Oracle identifies `DESede` as Triple DES; it is a standard Java algorithm name even though it is outside this CrySL rule’s list. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html

## Documented usage and remediation

- The class is for raw secret keys representable as byte arrays without associated key parameters. Constructors copy the supplied bytes. They reject null or empty key material and a null algorithm; the slice constructor also checks the stated bounds conditions. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))
- **Neither constructor verifies that the bytes form a valid key for the named algorithm.** Oracle’s DES example says to use an algorithm-specific key specification when those algorithm-specific checks are needed. `DESedeKeySpec`, for example, documents a 24-byte key representation and a separate parity-checking method; its documentation does not claim that it performs every possible security check. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))
- The `SecretKeySpec` documentation does **not** prescribe replacing `DESede` with a particular algorithm or provide a general repair procedure for this diagnostic. Separately, NIST’s TDEA transition guidance disallows applying new cryptographic protection after December 31, 2023, while permitting processing of already-protected data, including decryption, key unwrapping and MAC verification. This is NIST guidance, not a constructor requirement. ([nist.gov](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2023/06/nist-withdraw-special-publication-800-67-revision-2))

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/DESedeKeySpec.html and https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2023/06/nist-withdraw-special-publication-800-67-revision-2

## Compatibility and migration limits

`getFormat()` reports `RAW`, and `getEncoded()` returns the key material. The class documentation does not specify a persisted application format, a wire format, or a conversion or migration path from DESede-protected data. It also does not say that merely changing the associated algorithm name converts a key or existing ciphertext. Consequently, compatibility with stored data and peers remains an unresolved, format-specific question. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

Oracle documents `SecretKeySpec` as available since Java SE 1.4. Actual algorithm, transformation, key-size and provider support must be checked against the target platform: for example, Java SE 25’s mandatory algorithm list includes particular AES and DESede transformations and key sizes. Those requirements are not a security-strength endorsement. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec.html))

## Exact rule in the supplied source

The source’s matching clauses are: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

```text
SPEC javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec

EVENTS
	c1: SecretKeySpec(keyMaterial, keyAlgorithm);
	c2: SecretKeySpec(keyMaterial, offset, len, keyAlgorithm);
	Con := c1 | c2;
```

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl

The declared type is `javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec`; the named events are its two- and four-argument construction forms. The parameter lists are specified, with `keyMaterial` declared `byte[]`, `keyAlgorithm` declared `java.lang.String`, and `offset` and `len` declared `int`. `ORDER` specifies `Con`.

**A method does not qualify under an express name-only matching clause in this source.** The source specifies the above construction events, not an arbitrary method sharing the name. It does not, by itself, document detector implementation or subtype-matching semantics, so whether an implementation could behave differently remains unresolved. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))

The rule constrains `keyAlgorithm` to `AES`, `HmacSHA256`, `HmacSHA384` or `HmacSHA512`; it also states the length and `neverTypeOf` constraints and requires `preparedKeyMaterial` or `randomized`. It ensures `speccedKey` and `generatedKey`. The source does not explain how `offset` and `len` are bound for the two-argument event, define the provenance predicates, or explain the additional spelling variants in the supplied diagnostic. The mutable source URL was inspected, but the supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeySpec.crysl))
